subject: Gartner says AI needs $8.5T and will get $3.6T
bodyMarkdown:
If there is a CPP line on your pay stub, you are already a lender to the AI build-out. On Wednesday a research firm put a number on how much of that build-out may never earn its money back.

## What Gartner actually counted

Gartner published a forecast on Wednesday saying more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to **impairment** by the end of 2030, which means the asset stays on the balance sheet while the owner admits it is worth less than it cost. The arithmetic behind that is checkable. Gartner's Will Sommer says owners of AI data centres would need roughly $8.5 trillion in cumulative revenue through 2030 to cover the capital spending they have already announced, their financing costs, and a 12 per cent return on the capital. Gartner expects AI revenue attributable to data centres to reach no more than $3.6 trillion over the same years. The firm also expects more than 80 per cent of **neocloud** providers, the companies that rent out GPUs by the hour instead of selling software, to stop operating independently by 2030. By 2032 the exposed figure grows to about $4 trillion.

## The bond market got there first

CoreWeave closed down 15.46 per cent at $65.78 on Wednesday. Nebius lost roughly 10 per cent and IREN about 12, and CNBC reported that traders spent the session buying put options on CoreWeave. The debt interests me more than the share price. CNBC's bond data had CoreWeave notes maturing in 2031 and 2032 yielding near 14.9 and 14.8 per cent, which is a market saying out loud it may not get paid back. Chief executive Mike Intrator sent a memo saying he is confident in a backlog that Forbes put around $104 billion, and that it more than supports all of the company's debt obligations. He may well be right. A backlog is a set of promises from customers who are themselves spending borrowed money, so it is worth whatever their balance sheets are worth. September CPI arrived the same morning at 3.7 per cent, up from 3.4 in August, which does nothing for anyone who needs cheap credit.

## Your CPP owns a piece of this

Here is the part that reaches Richmond Hill. The Globe and Mail reported in July that CPP Investments committed US$1.75 billion to an AI infrastructure strategy led by the Swedish firm EQT, with the money flowing into projects run by EdgeConneX. That sits on top of a US$15 billion joint venture with Equinix, US$1.3 billion into a data centre fund led by Ares Management, and a $225 million loan to an AI computing development in Cambridge, Ontario. Max Biagosch, who runs real assets at CPP Investments, described a sector held up by durable long-term demand. I do not think any of that is reckless. CPP is buying buildings and power, not hourly GPU rentals, and Gartner aimed its 80 per cent prediction at the renters. The renters are the tenants, though, and when tenants fold, landlords renegotiate.

## The takeaway

Watch the CoreWeave yields rather than the stock, because a bond stuck above 14 per cent is what eventually decides how much gets built. The big cloud companies report later this month, and the line to find is the depreciation schedule on AI hardware, since stretching the assumed useful life of a GPU is the cleanest way to make a year's profit look fine. If you hold a Canadian or American index fund you own this trade through several doors already, and the question worth sitting with is whether you meant to. Gartner is a research firm with subscriptions to sell, so treat $3.5 trillion as one scenario rather than a count.
